Listen to this article Share Cryptocurrency’s two-year streak of political good fortune in the U.S. capital has ended abruptly. This is coming as Democrats’ midterm sweep of both the House and Senate has left the industry confronting tougher regulatory scrutiny and intensified examination of its close ties to president Donald Trump. For the past two years, digital-asset firms enjoyed a rare alignment of interests in Washington. Trump elevated crypto as a national priority, regulators eased enforcement paths that had constrained the sector under the prior administration, and a Republican-led Congress advanced elements of the industry’s agenda. Spot bitcoin exchange-traded funds flourished, banking access improved, a federal stablecoin framework took shape, and the administration explored a strategic bitcoin reserve. Read also: Explainer: What CBN’s new crypto rules mean for your wallet, P2P trades and stablecoins Trump and his family simultaneously built substantial personal crypto holdings, including the official TRUMP memecoin and World Liberty Financial, a decentralized finance and stablecoin venture that generated hundreds of millions in reported revenue. That favorable climate shifted decisively after the November 3 elections. Democrats flipped control of both chambers, a result that prediction markets had partially anticipated for the House but that delivered sharper losses for Republicans in the Senate than many expected. Key industry-friendly Republican lawmakers fell, while crypto skeptics, including former Senate Banking Committee chair Sherrod Brown in Ohio, returned or retained influence. Industry super PAC Fairshake and allied groups had spent well over $150 million this cycle, and more than $300 million across recent cycles, backing candidates from both parties. Despite winning many targeted races, the overall map left Democrats in charge of the legislative calendar and committee gavels. The immediate casualty is comprehensive market-structure legislation. The Clarity Act, which sought to clarify whether digital assets fall primarily under the Securities and Exchange Commission or the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, passed the House in 2025 but stalled in the Senate on a 49-50 procedural vote in September. Analysts at TD Cowen and others now judge the bill effectively dead for the next two years in anything resembling its current form. Any future version would require Democratic support and would likely incorporate stronger consumer protections, ethics restrictions, and oversight provisions the industry has resisted. Committee leadership changes amplify the pressure. Senator Elizabeth Warren is positioned to chair the Senate Banking Committee, giving one of crypto’s most consistent critics agenda-setting power over digital-asset legislation and oversight. In the House, Representative Maxine Waters is expected to reclaim the Financial Services Committee gavel. Both have long argued that existing rules insufficiently address investor risks, market manipulation, and conflicts of interest. Incoming House Oversight leaders have already signaled interest in examining the Trump family’s crypto activities. Scrutiny of those personal ties is set to intensify. Democrats have highlighted Trump’s financial disclosures showing more than $1 billion in crypto-related income in 2025, including substantial royalties from the TRUMP memecoin and proceeds linked to World Liberty Financial. Reuters and other outlets have estimated the family’s broader crypto earnings at $2.3 billion or higher since mid-2024. Particular attention focuses on a reported roughly $500 million investment by an Abu Dhabi-linked vehicle that acquired a significant stake in World Liberty Financial around the time of Trump’s inauguration, as well as the October 2025 pardon of Binance founder Changpeng Zhao. Democrats have questioned potential conflicts, national-security implications of foreign capital, and whether regulatory forbearance benefited politically connected projects. White House officials have dismissed the criticism as partisan attacks, insisting no conflicts exist. Industry executives and lobbyists are recalibrating. Coinbase policy officials and others have stressed that crypto retains bipartisan support and that many newly elected members remain open to innovation-friendly rules. Yet the shift forces a pivot from offense to defense against investigations and potential restrictive amendments. Oversight hearings, document requests, and possible subpoenas targeting World Liberty Financial, related stablecoins, and agency handling of the sector are widely expected once the new Congress convenes in January. Markets registered the political change with an initial sell-off followed by a partial recovery. Bitcoin briefly touched multi-week lows near $75,600 before rebounding toward the high $70,000s and low $80,000s as traders assessed that divided government and presidential veto power would limit radical policy reversals. Trump-linked tokens, however, suffered steeper declines, underscoring the political premium that had attached to them. Read also: Binance hack exposes risks in Nigeria’s $59bn crypto market The broader backdrop remains challenging. The crypto market has already shed hundreds of billions in value in recent months amid a major exchange hack, ETF outflows, and macroeconomic headwinds. The loss of a unified pro-crypto political tailwind removes one source of optimism just as institutional adoption continues to mature. For an industry that spent heavily to shape a durable bipartisan coalition intended to outlast any single administration, the midterm results mark a sobering reset. The extraordinary alignment of a crypto-friendly White House, sympathetic regulators, and a cooperative Congress has given way to divided government and heightened skepticism. Tougher rules, closer examination of political connections, and a more contested path for legislation now define the near-term outlook in Washington. How skillfully the sector navigates this new reality will help determine whether the gains of the past two years prove durable or temporary.
